blocks.text:
Design a Snake and Ladder Game for two or more players on a numbered board. Players take turns rolling a dice and moving forward, automatically sliding down any snake they land on, or climbing any ladder they land on, until someone reaches the final cell exactly.

  • Actors: two or more players taking turns.
  • Scope: a single board with a configurable size, plus a set of snakes and ladders.
  • Goal: guarantee every board configuration is internally consistent, and every turn correctly applies dice, snakes, ladders and the win condition.

The one rule this entire system exists to enforce: a player only wins by landing on the exact final cell, and every snake or ladder always resolves the same way, every single time. Everything else supports that.

items: The system shall support two or more players taking turns in order.
The system shall roll a dice each turn and move the current player forward by that amount.
If a player lands on a snake, the system shall move them down to the snake’s tail automatically.
If a player lands on a ladder, the system shall move them up to the ladder’s top automatically.
A roll that would move a player past the final cell shall be rejected, forfeiting that turn.
The system shall declare a winner the moment a player lands exactly on the final cell.

metadata.alt: Four non-functional priorities: fairness, extensibility, observability and configuration validity

items: Fairness: every player’s roll must go through the exact same dice rule, no player gets special treatment.
Extensibility: it should be possible to swap in a different dice rule (two dice, a weighted dice) without touching the core game loop.
Observability: every snake bite, ladder climb and win must be visible to anything watching the game, not buried inside internal logic.
Validity: a board’s snake and ladder configuration must be checked for internal consistency before the game ever starts.
Thread Safety: two near-simultaneous turn submissions must never corrupt whose turn it actually is.
How many players does the game need to support, a fixed two, or an arbitrary number?
What should happen if a roll would take a player past the final cell, forfeit the turn, or clamp to the final cell?
Should the board size and snake/ladder layout be configurable, or fixed at a standard 100 cells?
Do we need to support multiple dice (e.g. rolling two dice and summing them)?
Is a single game session enough, or do we need to persist and resume an in-progress game?
A roll that would overshoot the final cell forfeits the turn entirely, the player stays exactly where they were, matching the most common house rule.
The board size and every snake/ladder position are configurable at game creation time via BoardFactory.
A single 1-6 dice is used by default, but the dice mechanism itself is pluggable.
The game supports two or more players, turn order is simply the order they were registered in.
Persistence between sessions is out of scope for the core game loop, a database design is still covered separately.

metadata.alt: SnakeAndLadderGame composing a Board, a DiceStrategy, Players, and notifying GameListeners

items: Board: the fixed size and snake/ladder layout every player moves across.
DiceStrategy: however a roll value gets produced, random or otherwise.
Player: a name and a current position on the board.
GameListener: anything that wants to react to a snake bite, ladder climb, or win.
SnakeAndLadderGame: the orchestrator tying turns, rolls, movement and events together.

metadata.alt: SnakeAndLadderGame composing a Board, using a DiceStrategy, and managing multiple Player instances

items: Composition: SnakeAndLadderGame composes its Board, the board has no purpose outside the specific game session that owns it.
Aggregation: the game aggregates its Player list, players could conceptually be reused across a rematch with a fresh board.
Association: the game is associated with a DiceStrategy and zero or more GameListeners, both swappable independently of the game’s own lifecycle.
Realization: FixedSequenceDiceStrategy realizes DiceStrategy; ConsoleGameListener realizes GameListener.

metadata.alt: SnakeAndLadderGame tying together Board, DiceStrategy, Player and GameListener

blocks.text: Notice that SnakeAndLadderGame never directly touches dice-rolling logic or snake/ladder lookup logic itself, both are delegated to DiceStrategy and Board respectively. This separation is exactly what keeps the game loop itself simple and stable.
Three patterns keep this design flexible and correct.

metadata.alt: DiceStrategy as the shared contract behind both a deterministic test strategy and a real random strategy

blocks.text: Why needed: real gameplay needs genuine randomness, but tests and demos need fully reproducible rolls. Why best: SnakeAndLadderGame only ever calls dice.roll(), it has no idea whether that roll is random or scripted. What it solves: lets the exact same game loop run identically whether it is being played for real or being verified for correctness.

metadata.alt: SnakeAndLadderGame notifying every registered GameListener of snake bites, ladder climbs and wins

blocks.text: Why needed: a console UI, a web UI, and an analytics tracker might all want to know about the same events, without the game itself needing to know any of them exist. Why best: new listener types (a stats tracker, a replay recorder) can be added freely with zero changes to SnakeAndLadderGame. What it solves: keeps event reporting fully decoupled from game logic.

metadata.alt: BoardFactory validating a snake and ladder layout before producing a usable Board

blocks.text: Why needed: a snake or ladder pointing the wrong direction, or two entries on the same cell, would silently corrupt gameplay if not caught immediately. Why best: BoardFactory is the single place all of this validation lives, a Board can never exist in an invalid state. What it solves: guarantees every Board the game ever plays on is already known to be internally consistent.

items: Board: responsibility is knowing the board size and resolving any cell to its true final position. Attributes: size, snakesAndLadders. Methods: getSize(), getFinalPosition().
BoardFactory: responsibility is validating a proposed layout before a Board is created. Methods: createBoard() (static).
Player: responsibility is holding a name and a current position. Attributes: name, position. Methods: getName(), getPosition(), setPosition().
SnakeAndLadderGame: responsibility is running turns and coordinating rolls, movement, and events. Attributes: board, dice, players, currentPlayerIndex, listeners. Methods: addListener(), playTurn().

metadata.alt: DiceStrategy and GameListener as the two extension points, each with one concrete implementation shown

blocks.text: DiceStrategy isolates how a roll is produced, letting real randomness and scripted testing coexist behind one contract. GameListener isolates reactions to game events, letting any number of independent observers watch the same game without coupling to each other.
Three workflows matter most: a ladder climb, a snake bite, and an overshoot that wastes a turn.

metadata.alt: A roll of 3 landing exactly on a ladder start, moving the player up to the ladder’s top

blocks.text: The dice value is added to the player’s position first, only afterward does the board check whether that landing cell has a ladder on it.

metadata.alt: A roll landing exactly on a snake’s head, moving the player down to the snake’s tail

blocks.text: The mechanism is symmetric to a ladder, the only difference is whether the resolved final position is higher or lower than where the dice roll originally landed.

metadata.alt: A roll that would move a player past the final cell, forfeiting the turn entirely

blocks.text: This is the one case where the board is never even consulted, the overshoot check happens first, and the turn simply passes to the next player unchanged.

metadata.alt: The full turn sequence: roll, check for overshoot, move, resolve snakes and ladders, advance to the next player

items: Happy path, plain move: the roll lands on a cell with no snake or ladder, the player simply advances that many cells.
Happy path, ladder climb: the roll lands exactly on a ladder’s start cell, the player is moved up to the ladder’s top instead.
Happy path, snake bite: the roll lands exactly on a snake’s head cell, the player is moved down to the snake’s tail instead.
Failure, overshoot: the roll would move the player past the final cell, the turn is forfeited and play passes to the next player unchanged.
SnakeAndLadderGame.playTurn(): plays exactly one turn for the current player, returns whether that turn won the game.
SnakeAndLadderGame.addListener(GameListener): registers a new observer for game events.
Board.getFinalPosition(int position): resolves a raw landing cell to where the player actually ends up.
BoardFactory.createBoard(size, snakes, ladders): the only way to construct a Board, guaranteeing it is valid.

metadata.alt: BoardFactory rejecting an invalid snake, ladder, or overlapping configuration before a Board can exist

items: Invalid input: a snake configured to move a player upward, or a ladder configured to move a player downward, is rejected immediately at board creation.
Resource unavailable: not directly applicable to the in-memory version, a persisted variant would need to handle a failed save gracefully.
Business-rule violation: a cell configured as both a snake start and a ladder start is rejected at board creation, this ambiguity can never reach actual gameplay.
System failure: a broken game listener throwing an exception should be caught per-listener, not allowed to prevent the player’s position from updating correctly.

metadata.alt: Two near-simultaneous turn submissions both needing to safely read and update the shared turn state

blocks.text: playTurn() reads and writes currentPlayerIndex and a player’s position together, if two turn requests are processed concurrently (a double-tap in a UI, or two client connections for the same session), the turn order or position updates can interleave incorrectly. The entire playTurn() call must be synchronized around a single lock, exactly as with the earlier problems in this series.

items: Supporting two dice summed together requires only a new DiceStrategy implementation, zero changes to SnakeAndLadderGame.
Supporting a "must roll exact number to win" house rule (rejecting an overshoot differently) would be a small, isolated change inside playTurn(), not a redesign.
Adding a StatsTrackingListener that counts snake bites and ladder climbs per player is a pure GameListener implementation, no core changes needed.
Future work: supporting a resumable, persisted game would add a serialization layer around SnakeAndLadderGame’s state, without changing the turn logic itself.
Single Responsibility: Board only resolves cells, BoardFactory only validates layouts, DiceStrategy only produces rolls, SnakeAndLadderGame only orchestrates turns.
Open/Closed: new dice rules and listener types can be added without modifying SnakeAndLadderGame’s existing, already-correct logic.
Liskov Substitution: any DiceStrategy or GameListener implementation can be substituted freely without SnakeAndLadderGame needing to know which one it has.
Interface Segregation: DiceStrategy exposes exactly one method, GameListener exposes exactly the three events it genuinely needs to report.
Dependency Inversion: SnakeAndLadderGame depends on the DiceStrategy and GameListener abstractions, never on a specific concrete implementation.

A roll that lands exactly on the final cell wins immediately, even if that same cell is also (incorrectly) configured as a snake or ladder start, board validation should already prevent this at setup time.
A single-player game (no real opponent): the game still functions, currentPlayerIndex simply always resolves back to the same player.

A snake or ladder chain (landing on one ladder’s top which is itself another snake’s head): this design resolves only ONE hop per turn, chaining is explicitly out of scope and worth calling out to an interviewer.
A board with zero snakes and zero ladders: still a fully valid, playable game, BoardFactory has nothing to reject.
DiceStrategy.roll(): O(1) for both the random and fixed-sequence implementations.
Board.getFinalPosition(): O(1), a direct hash map lookup.
SnakeAndLadderGame.playTurn(): O(k) where k is the number of registered listeners, dominated by event notification.
Space: O(number of snakes and ladders) for the board’s lookup map, plus O(number of players) for game state.

metadata.alt: GAME tracking BOARD_CONFIG, its SNAKE_OR_LADDER entries, and every PLAYER_STATE

blocks.text: Persisting a game in progress needs three things: GAME stores the overall session and board size, BOARD_CONFIG and SNAKE_OR_LADDER capture the exact layout being played on, and PLAYER_STATE tracks every player’s current position so a game can be reconstructed and resumed exactly as it was left.

items: How would you support snake/ladder chains, where landing on one leads immediately into another?
How would you add a computer-controlled player that plays automatically without a human submitting turns?
How would you extend this to support a shared, resumable multiplayer session across multiple devices?
How would you test that a randomly generated board layout can never contain a contradictory snake/ladder configuration?

codes.python:
# Orchestrates the whole game: whose turn it is, rolling, moving,
# checking for snakes/ladders, and notifying listeners of every event
class SnakeAndLadderGame:
    def __init__(self, board, dice, players):
        self.board = board                    # the fixed board layout
        self.dice = dice                       # however dice rolls are produced
        self.players = players                 # every player in turn order
        self.current_player_index = 0          # the first player in the list goes first
        self.listeners = []                    # everyone watching for events

    def add_listener(self, listener):
        self.listeners.append(listener)  # register a new observer, does not replace existing ones

    def play_turn(self):
        # Plays exactly one turn for whichever player is currently up.
        # Returns True only if that turn caused someone to win.
        player = self.players[self.current_player_index]  # whose turn is it
        roll = self.dice.roll()                            # ask the dice strategy for a value
        new_position = player.position + roll              # where would this roll take them

        if new_position > self.board.get_size():
            # overshooting the final cell is not allowed, this turn is simply wasted
            self.current_player_index = (self.current_player_index + 1) % len(self.players)
            return False  # nobody won on a wasted turn

        # ask the board whether this landing cell has a snake or ladder on it
        final_position = self.board.get_final_position(new_position)

        if final_position < new_position:
            # landed lower than where the dice roll put them: a snake bit them
            for listener in self.listeners:
                listener.on_snake_bite(player, new_position, final_position)
        elif final_position > new_position:
            # landed higher than where the dice roll put them: a ladder was climbed
            for listener in self.listeners:
                listener.on_ladder_climb(player, new_position, final_position)
        # if final_position equals new_position, nothing special happened, no event fires

        player.position = final_position  # actually update the player's position now

        if final_position == self.board.get_size():
            # reaching the exact final cell means this player has won
            for listener in self.listeners:
                listener.on_player_won(player)
            return True  # signal to the caller that the game is over

        self.current_player_index = (self.current_player_index + 1) % len(self.players)  # pass the turn along
        return False  # game continues

items: Why does BoardFactory reject an invalid layout instead of Board simply ignoring bad entries at lookup time? Because catching the mistake once, at setup, is far safer than silently producing wrong gameplay behavior on every future lookup of that cell.

Why is the overshoot rule (forfeit the turn) checked before the board is ever consulted for snakes or ladders? Because a position past the final cell is not even a valid board position, there is nothing meaningful to look up yet.

Why does the demo use FixedSequenceDiceStrategy instead of RandomDiceStrategy? Because a design document’s example output needs to be exactly reproducible, this is exactly the kind of testing concern the Strategy pattern was chosen to support.

An alternative could store the board as an actual array of 100 cells rather than a sparse map of just the snakes and ladders, simpler mental model, but wastes memory on a board where almost every cell has no special behavior.

A simpler design could skip the Observer pattern and just have playTurn() return an event object describing what happened, less flexible for supporting multiple simultaneous listeners, but avoids the small overhead of a notification loop.

Supporting snake and ladder chaining (resolving repeatedly until landing on a plain cell) was deliberately left out, real Snake and Ladder implementations vary on this rule, and resolving it explicitly in one place keeps the core loop’s behavior unambiguous.
Persist the board layout and player positions (already modeled in the ER diagram) so a game can survive a server restart mid-session.
Validate turn submissions come from the actual current player, never trust a client to only submit on its own turn.
Log every snake bite, ladder climb, and win (the same events GameListener already exposes) for analytics on which layouts produce the most exciting games.
Consider rate-limiting turn submissions per session to prevent a buggy client from spamming playTurn() calls.
